transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-06
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Kumar (Statera Head of Platform), Liam O'Neal (Security Architect), Sofia Ramos (Compliance Manager)

Summary:
Quick discovery to establish Statera's geofencing/data residency constraints and audit/logging obligations for an LLM-based payments assistant. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC / on-prem) with strict EU/US segmentation and PCI-ish controls plus SOC2/HIPAA adjacent concerns. They want clear evidence of log flows, KMS residency, and audit chains before engaging for a pilot.

Topics:
- Regional locking / geofencing of requests and model inference
- Audit logs, PII redaction, and retention windows
- KMS / HSM residency and key flow for Private deployments
- Tradeoffs: latency/cost for Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private
- Benchmarking and proof artifacts required for internal compliance

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on this end, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Priya Kumar: Doing well, thanks. Busy week — appreciate you making time.
[00:16] Diego Alvarez: Thanks, Priya. Quick agenda from our side: get a sense of the data boundaries, what compliance gates you need, and then we can map Redwood deployment options to those constraints. Is that ok?
[00:26] Sofia Ramos: That's perfect. To be blunt, we can't ship anything that moves EU personal data outside the EU. Also the payments metadata needs to be auditable and we have to show an immutable audit chain for certain flows.
[00:38] Liam O'Neal: And we have, um, strong requirements around who can see raw transcripts or logs. We need to understand where those logs live and how they're encrypted.
[00:46] Maya Chen: Great, thank you. Just so we're aligned on terms — when you say "move outside the EU" do you mean inference compute, logs, and key material all must remain in the EU? Or is there a subset?
[00:57] Priya Kumar: Everything. Inference compute, KV cache, model weights not allowed to leave EU, and if possible keys must be under our KMS, EU region HSM. We also want logs scrubbed of PAN and cardholder elements before any off-site storage.
[01:12] Diego Alvarez: Understood. A couple quick clarifying q's — are you open to running Redwood Dedicated in an EU cloud region, or are you more leaning to Redwood Private (VPC) or even on-prem?
[01:23] Priya Kumar: Prefer private VPC first. If that doesn't meet our latency and throughput we might consider a hybrid where the inference stays in EU dedicated pools. But private VPC is the bar.
[01:34] Sofia Ramos: Also, we need SSO integration and RBAC mapped to our IdP — SAML is fine. And audit logs must have user-level tracing tied to our SSO identities.
[01:45] Diego Alvarez: Makes sense. Technically we can do SAML SSO and map RBAC. For logging we have a few models: local audit logs that you retain, optional ship-to-customer-S3 in your region, and redact-before-export. Our redaction is rule-based and also we can apply custom regex filters — though very long-running streaming transcripts can be tricky for perfect redaction.
[02:07] Liam O'Neal: When you say redact-before-export, is that happening on the inference host, or in the control plane? We can't have raw transcripts leave the VPC unredacted.
[02:16] Diego Alvarez: Right. For Redwood Private VPC, the inference node can run the redaction step locally — we call the hook pre-export. There's a small risk window if we stream to the control plane for management telemetry but we can configure telemetry to strip payloads and only send token-level metrics.
[02:31] Priya Kumar: Are there docs we can see that show the exact dataflow?
[02:34] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send a region-locked deployment diagram and the control plane separation doc. We'll include the difference between Dedicated (tenant-isolated pools in our region), Hosted (multi-tenant with region controls), and Private (customer VPC + private control plane).
[02:46] Sophia Ramos: You said tenant-isolated for Dedicated — can you guarantee no data egress to Redwood control plane in that mode?
[02:54] Diego Alvarez: There's a nuance — Dedicated uses our reserved GPU pools and a control plane for orchestration. By default, some metadata and usage metrics are sent to control plane but payloads can be configured to never leave the dedicated environment. For customers wanting zero egress, Private VPC or on-prem is the path.
[03:12] Liam O'Neal: Ok. What about KMS — can we bring our own keys and restrict key operations to EU-only HSM?
[03:19] Maya Chen: Yes, we support customer-managed keys. For Private we can integrate with your KMS (Cloud KMS/HSM) so key material never leaves your control. For Dedicated we can also configure CMEK but some ops like backups need to be discussed.
[03:32] Priya Kumar: Backup snapshots are a pain. We need to know if model weights or KV cache backups could leak anything. We treat model cache as potentially sensitive because of prompt kernels and payment tokens.
[03:44] Diego Alvarez: Good point. We can turn off persistent KV backups or ensure they are encrypted under your CMEK and stored in your region. Note that some performance-optimized runtimes may rely on local cached checkpoints — we can isolate those to encrypted ephemeral storage.
[03:58] Sofia Ramos: About logs — retention policy is 7 years for some records. Are you able to support long retention in the customer's storage?
[04:07] Diego Alvarez: We can ship logs to your S3/GCS in-region and you can set lifecycle rules. Redwood's built-in retention defaults are shorter but enterprise add-on supports extended retention.
[04:18] Priya Kumar: On the audit chain, can you provide an immutable tamper-evident log? We currently use append-only logs with signed entries.
[04:28] Diego Alvarez: We have a feature for cryptographic signing of logs and we can push signed bundles to your archive location. It's not a full blockchain but it gives tamper evidence with signatures and sequence numbers.
[04:39] Liam O'Neal: Ok that helps. Another thing — PCI scope. We're not asking for PCI compliance from Redwood yet, but we need to make sure using your inference doesn't expand our PCI scope uncontrollably.
[04:51] Maya Chen: Totally. We're careful about that. Our recommended pattern is to tokenize card data before it hits the model layer, and ensure the tokenization service is in your PCI zone. We can also offer a pre-filter to drop PANs.
[05:03] Priya Kumar: Good. Could you outline the differences in unit economics? If we go Private VPC in EU region vs Dedicated reserved pools, what's the tradeoff for latency and cost?
[05:15] Diego Alvarez: Sure — Private VPC tends to have slightly higher fixed setup and networking egress cost, but gives you full control over residency and keys. Dedicated reserved pools reduce per-token cost at scale but still have some control plane interactions; latency can be slightly better in Dedicated because we operate optimized kernels and pooling, but Private can be tuned similarly if we deploy the same runtime profile. We'll send a cost sketch with examples.
[05:37] Sofia Ramos: Are there existing customers in payments who've done Private with EU-only keys? We like references.
[05:44] Maya Chen: We can share an anonymized case study and a reference call — can't give live customer PII but we'll provide sanitized references and a contact if eligible.
[05:53] Priya Kumar: For the pilot, our must-haves: EU-only inference and logs, CMEK in EU, SAML SSO mapping, pre-export redaction rules, and an audit signature chain. If you can tick those boxes, we'll move to POC scoping.
[06:07] Diego Alvarez: Sounds achievable. For the POC we'll propose a week-long throughput and latency benchmark with your sample traffic, plus a security review. We'll also test redaction accuracy against a sample prompt set.
[06:20] Liam O'Neal: On the security review — we need pen test evidence, SOC 2 Type II, and answers to our questionnaire. Can you share the standard security pack now?
[06:30] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll email the security pack after this call; it includes SOC2, ISO summaries, penetration testing cadence, and our compliance whitepaper.
[06:38] Sofia Ramos: Also please include a template export of logs so we can validate fields and sequence numbers.
[06:44] Maya Chen: Will do. Diego, any technical caveats to call out now?
[06:48] Diego Alvarez: Two small caveats: 1) real-time streaming with pre-export redaction adds a bit of latency depending on the complexity of regexes, and 2) some quantized model variants have different deterministic characteristics which can affect traceability — not a blocker, just something to capture in the POC.
[07:06] Priya Kumar: That last bit about quantized models and determinism — can you explain quickly?
[07:11] Diego Alvarez: Sure. Some of the low-bit quantized models we support run faster but produce slightly more variance in outputs for identical prompts due to different arithmetic. For auditability we usually recommend a stable variant for canonical logging depending on the use case.
[07:26] Liam O'Neal: Makes sense. Any integration hooks for our SIEM? We want syslog or structured events to land in Splunk.
[07:35] Maya Chen: We support pushing structured events to your SIEM via webhook, Kinesis, or direct S3 ingestion with CloudTrail-style records.
[07:44] Priya Kumar: Great. Let's talk timeline — we want a POC started by end of October ideally. We need to brief execs next Tuesday.
[07:53] Maya Chen: We can aim for a POC kickoff the week of 2026-10-26. I'll follow up with a proposed plan and resource needs.
[07:59] Sofia Ramos: Cool. Any final questions?
[08:02] Liam O'Neal: No from me. We'll await the security pack and the region design doc.
[08:07] Maya Chen: Perfect. Recap of next steps: I'll send SOC2/ISO docs and region map; Diego will draft the Private VPC runbook and redaction pattern doc; Priya will share the dataflow diagram. We'll schedule the architecture workshop mid-next week.
[08:21] Priya Kumar: Thanks, everyone. Helpful call.
[08:24] Maya Chen: Thanks all. End call.

Notes on transcript quality: Automatic transcription had some entity swapping ("KV cache" transcribed as "K-V cash" in one place), and a couple of names were shortened; audio quality medium but content is intact.
